IR.rationale: A steepening curve without a rise at the front end points to better growth expectations without monetary tightening. That reflationary state supports global equity cash-flow expectations.

B.rationale: Narrowing spreads together with strong high-yield returns mark easing credit conditions and rising risk appetite. Corporate bond and equity risk premia share common drivers that carry across borders.

V.rationale: High implied volatility carries a large variance and equity risk premium. Elevated VIX has been documented to predict higher subsequent global equity returns over weeks to months.

AP.rationale: US market returns lead other developed markets' returns, as documented in research on the predictive role of the US market. Global time-series momentum adds to that effect at short horizons.

ST.rationale: Weak momentum returns tend to coincide with junk rallies and rebounds after drawdowns. This makes the momentum factor a coarse signal of the market's turning state.

FX.rationale: A weakening dollar together with a strong commodity currency marks a global risk-on, easier dollar-funding state. That state favours non-US equities, especially in dollar terms.

COM.rationale: Broad commodity gains signal stronger global demand. Europe and Asia have large cyclical and resource sectors that benefit from it.

MC.rationale: High financial stress raises required risk premia and marks states with depressed prices. In such states subsequent expected returns differ systematically from normal times.

ENDG.rationale: Equity indices show time-series momentum at horizons of one to twelve months. Recent strength therefore carries information about the next weeks.

IR.rationale: Sharp falls in bill yields reflect flight-to-quality demand and expected policy easing in response to stress. Both precede turbulent equity markets.

B.rationale: Widening spreads with falling high-yield prices signal deteriorating credit and funding conditions. Through the leverage and credit channel these predict higher equity volatility.

V.rationale: Implied volatility contains forward-looking information about future realised variance beyond its own history. Global equity volatilities are tightly linked to the VIX.

AP.rationale: Joint declines in US and emerging equities signal a global sell-off. Through the leverage effect and volatility feedback, falls raise subsequent volatility asymmetrically.

ST.rationale: High short-term reversal returns reflect high returns to liquidity provision. Those returns arise when markets are disorderly and liquidity is scarce, conditions that persist into higher volatility.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation with commodity-currency weakness is the signature of carry-trade unwinding and global deleveraging. That state is associated with spikes in equity volatility.

COM.rationale: Broad commodity declines signal falling global demand and risk-off flows. Such states tend to precede more volatile equity markets.

MC.rationale: Financial stress coinciding with a deteriorating labour market marks a recessionary stress state. Stock market volatility is markedly higher and more persistent in such states.

ENDG.rationale: Volatility is persistent and partly nonlinear, so very high recent variance carries extra information. Long-memory effects of that kind go beyond a linear autoregression.

IR.rationale: A falling medium-term rate relative to the policy rate signals a growth scare and expected easing. Such scares precede equity drawdowns.

B.rationale: Credit deterioration tends to lead equity crashes. Widening spreads and falling junk prices indicate rising default risk and tightening funding.

V.rationale: High market fear combined with high policy uncertainty widens the left tail of the return distribution. Large losses cluster in such high-volatility regimes.

AP.rationale: US market declines transmit to other developed markets with a lag. Crashes are contagious and cluster across markets.

ST.rationale: Momentum underperformance accompanies turning points and deleveraging episodes. In those episodes broad equity drawdowns are more likely.

FX.rationale: A rising yen with a falling Australian dollar indicates carry unwinding and global risk aversion. Carry-trade crash risk is tied to equity crash risk.

COM.rationale: Oil price collapses signal weakening global demand and stress in energy credit. Both raise downside risk for cyclical non-US markets.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress indicates impaired intermediation. Large equity losses are much more frequent in such states.

ENDG.rationale: Poor recent returns raise the chance of further large losses. Volatility clustering and short-horizon momentum both work in that direction.

IR.rationale: Curve steepening reflects improving growth expectations or easing. Both precede strong equity rallies.

B.rationale: Strong high-yield returns signal recovering risk appetite and easing credit stress. Sharp equity rebounds tend to follow.

V.rationale: Large gains, like large losses, cluster in high-volatility regimes. Rebound rallies occur when risk premia are elevated.

AP.rationale: Strong emerging-market equities signal global risk-on and growth momentum. These spill over to Europe and developed Asia.

ST.rationale: Momentum crashes coincide with violent rallies led by past losers after market declines. They mark rebound states.

FX.rationale: Dollar weakness with commodity-currency strength marks easing global dollar funding and risk-on flows. That state favours big gains in non-US equities.

COM.rationale: A broad commodity rally signals reflation and global demand recovery. Resource-heavy and cyclical non-US markets benefit.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress without real-economy deterioration describes overdone fear. Sharp relief rallies are likely in that state.

ENDG.rationale: After large declines, return dispersion and the chance of sharp rebounds rise. Volatility clustering and reversal of extreme moves both contribute.
